title: The Relational Model and Relational Algebra
summary: Presents the relational model's structures and integrity rules, relational algebra operators, and criteria for a fully relational database system.

concepts.title: Domains and relations
concepts.summary: A domain defines valid atomic values, while a relation organizes domain values into uniquely identifiable rows and named columns.

concepts.title: Degree and cardinality
concepts.summary: A relation's degree is its number of columns and its cardinality is its number of rows.

concepts.title: Relational keys
concepts.summary: Candidate keys can uniquely identify rows; one becomes the primary key, the others are alternate keys, and foreign keys represent relationships.

concepts.title: Entity integrity
concepts.summary: No component of a primary key may be null because every row must remain identifiable.

concepts.title: Referential integrity
concepts.summary: A foreign key must be null when optional or match an existing referenced key value.

concepts.title: Restrict and project
concepts.summary: Restrict selects rows and project selects columns, producing new relations without changing the source relation.

concepts.title: Relational set operators
concepts.summary: Union, intersect, and difference combine union-compatible relations according to set membership.

concepts.title: Product and join
concepts.summary: Product creates every row pairing, while join retains pairings that satisfy a related-value condition.

concepts.title: Divide and relational completeness
concepts.summary: Divide expresses all-related-to queries, and a language is relationally complete if it can express every relational algebra operation.

concepts.title: Data independence
concepts.summary: Relational systems aim to shield applications from changes in physical storage and information-preserving logical design.

concepts.title: Fully relational behavior
concepts.summary: Relational-system rules cover table-based representation, guaranteed access, null handling, catalogs, integrity, set-level operations, and independence.
